text:
The fog wasn’t just gray; it was the color of forgotten memories, thick and viscous. Elias wiped his spectacles, expecting the usual swirl of mist against the glass. Instead, he saw a school of neon-blue jellyfish drifting through the air, their translucent bells pulsing in rhythm with the lighthouse beam. They didn’t float; they swam upstream, defying gravity, leaving trails of phosphorescent slime that sizzled when they touched the iron railing.

Elias froze. He had spent forty years watching ships, not sky-creatures. Then, one jellyfish detached from the group and floated toward the lantern room window. It pressed its gelatinous tentacles against the glass, and inside Elias’s head, a voice echoed—not words, but the sensation of drowning in warm tea. The creature blinked an eye made of starlight. Behind it, the fog began to peel back like old paint, revealing not the sea, but a vast, inverted ocean suspended in the clouds, teeming with whales made of smoke.

The lighthouse beam flickered, confused by this new horizon. Elias realized the light wasn’t guiding ships home anymore; it was trying to illuminate a world that existed only in the space between breaths. He reached for his logbook, pen trembling, as the first drop of rain fell upward, splashing against the ceiling.
